evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.26.3: cotīdiē aliquid legitur aut scrībitur
Cic. Sen. 38: senīle aliquid … aliquid adulēscentis
terms.comment: “Something old, something new” takes an agreeing adjective or a genitive: senīle aliquid, aliquid adulēscentis (Cic. Sen. 38). Lewis & Short (s.v. aliquis): aliquid says that the thing exists, though not which; quid leaves even that open.

terms.gloss: something, anything (after sī, nisi, num, nē)
evidence: Cic. Att. 15.16a: sī quid scrībere velīs
terms.comment: After sī, nisi, num and nē the ali- drops: sī quid, if anything; nē quid, so that nothing.

evidence: Cic. Att. 13.38.1: exarāvī nesciō quid ad tē

phrases.latin: sīc igitur vīvitur: cotīdiē aliquid legitur aut scrībitur
phrases.english: so this is how we live: every day something gets read or written

phrases.latin: ut enim adulēscentem in quō est senīle aliquid, sīc senem in quō est aliquid adulēscentis probō
phrases.english: as I like a young man with something of the old man in him, so I like an old man with something of the young

phrases.latin: sī quid forte abest, ipse vacuus locus admonet, ut, quod deest, requīrātur
phrases.english: if anything happens to be missing, the empty place itself reminds you to look for what is gone

sources: Lewis & Short: aliquis · Lewis & Short: quis · Lewis & Short: nescio · Lewis & Short: quidam
